hints: Look carefully at the two curves at the same partial pressure of oxygen. Which curve shows a higher percentage saturation of haemoglobin?
Remember what a shift to the left means: higher saturation at a low partial pressure shows haemoglobin is holding onto oxygen more strongly, which is vital where oxygen is scarce.
walkthrough:
**Read the graph carefully**

Pick any partial pressure of oxygen on the x-axis in the middle of the graph. Now go straight up to both curves.

You will see the high altitude curve is above and to the left of the low altitude curve. That means at the same $pO_2$, haemoglobin is more saturated with oxygen.

**Recall what left shift means**

A curve shifted to the left means haemoglobin loads oxygen easily even when oxygen is scarce.

We call this a higher affinity for oxygen. It is the opposite of releasing oxygen readily, which would be a shift to the right.

**Link to high altitude survival**

At high altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen in the air is very low, so loading oxygen in the lungs is difficult.

Having haemoglobin with a higher affinity is a great adaptation because it can still become well saturated even at that low $pO_2$.

options.A: Correct. The left shift shows higher percentage saturation at any given partial pressure, which means higher affinity for oxygen.
options.B: Releasing oxygen more readily would need a shift to the right (lower affinity), so haemoglobin unloads easily at respiring tissues. This is the opposite of what is shown.
options.C: The Bohr effect is a right shift caused by high carbon dioxide lowering pH, which helps release oxygen. It does not explain this left-shifted, high-affinity curve.
options.D: This describes a temporary physiological effect of low carbon dioxide, not the inherited adaptation of high-altitude animals to have high-affinity haemoglobin.
